::: {.part}
Part two · why slow works
:::

## The heart is already breathing with you {#rsa .stop data-stop="rsa"}

::: {.year}
Now, in you
:::

::: {.lead}
Your heart rate is not steady. It rises as you breathe in and falls as you breathe out, and
it is doing that at this moment.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014 [@lehrer14], and Russo and colleagues, 2017 [@russo17]. The pattern
has a name — **respiratory sinus arrhythmia** — and the 2014 review states it plainly:
heart rate "increases during inhalation and decreases during exhalation".

As solid as anything on these pages. It is directly observable in anyone, with any device
that reads a pulse, and it needs no statistics at all.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="rsa"}
Move through one breath. The direction is the established finding; the size of the swing
drawn here is illustrative, because yours depends on your age, your fitness and how slowly
you are breathing.
:::

If you have ever put a pulse oximeter on someone and watched the number wander, this is what
you were watching. It is not the device being imprecise.

Why it happens is a longer story than it looks, and the 2014 review is careful to say that
parts of the account are proposed rather than settled. The short version is that the same
brainstem machinery times the breath and adjusts the heart, and that the pressure sensors in
the big arteries — the
**[baroreflex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroreflex){.wiki}** — are correcting blood
pressure continuously as the chest changes shape around them.

The useful part for a practitioner is simpler. The breath is not a separate system you are
reaching in to influence. It is already wired to the heart, continuously, in everyone, and
what a breathing instruction does is change the timing of something that is happening anyway.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
This is the one claim on the page a client can check for themselves in thirty seconds with a
finger on their own wrist and a long slow breath. Things people verify on their own body
land differently from things they are told.
:::

## One rate rings louder than the others {#resonance .stop data-stop="resonance"}

::: {.year}
2014
:::

::: {.lead}
Breathe at about six a minute and the swing in your heart rate gets much bigger. Not
gradually bigger as you slow down — biggest at one particular rate, and smaller again either
side of it.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014 [@lehrer14]. "Maximum heart rate oscillations at respiratory
frequency occurred at approximately 0.1 Hz (six breaths per minute)", refined in the same
review to about **5.5 a minute**, a breath of roughly eleven seconds. Russo's review reports
the same peak [@russo17].

Where the peak sits is replicated and solid. The mechanism has a good account — and the
authors of the review are explicit that parts of it are speculation, including the newer
suggestion about signals travelling up the vagus nerve to the front of the brain.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="resonance"}
Find the peak. Where it sits is the established finding; the height of the hill is drawn
rather than measured, and how sharp yours is will not be quite this.
:::

Here is the part that makes it a **resonance** rather than just a good rate. Your blood
pressure is being corrected continuously by the baroreflex, and that correction takes a few
seconds to arrive. Breathe at around six a minute and each breath's push lands just as the
correction from the last one comes through — heart rate and blood pressure end up running
**half a cycle apart**, blood pressure falling as heart rate rises. The timing is what does
it: every push adds to the swing already there instead of fighting it.

It is the same reason a child on a swing goes higher when the pushes are timed to the swing
rather than delivered faster. The system has a natural period, and matching it costs nothing
and does more.

What this does **not** establish is what people usually go on to say. A bigger swing in heart
rate is a real physiological change, and it is a measurement, not an outcome. The step from
*this makes your heart rate variation larger* to *this makes you healthier* is the step part
three is about, and it is much less secure than this stop.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
If you are going to give someone a number, six a minute is the one with the most behind it —
in through the nose for about four seconds, out for about six, and no straining at either
end. Longer out than in is the part most people find easiest to hold on to.
:::

## And it is not the same rate for everybody {#predicts .stop data-stop="predicts"}

::: {.year}
2006
:::

::: {.lead}
Six a minute is the average of a spread, not a setting. People have their own rate, it can
be found, and it stays put.
:::

::: {.src}
[The research]{.lbl}
Vaschillo, Vaschillo & Lehrer, 2006 [@vaschillo06] — 32 adults with asthma and 24 healthy
adults, each tested to find the rate at which their own heart rate swung most.

One laboratory, 56 people, and the findings are reported as **directions** rather than as
numbers — which is why the figure shows directions and no numbers. Good enough to say the
spread is real and roughly what predicts it. Not good enough to give anyone a formula.
:::

::: {.journey-figure data-scene="predicts"}
What predicted a person's own best rate, and what did not. No numbers on this figure,
deliberately — the paper does not publish the coefficients and inventing them would be
worse than leaving them out.
:::

Taller people resonated at a slower rate, and men slower than women — which is very likely
the same finding twice, since the paper relates it to blood volume rather than to sex as
such. Age did not predict it. Weight did not. Having asthma did not.

And the finding that matters most for anyone teaching this: a person's rate **stayed the
same across ten sessions**. It is a stable property of them, like a resting heart rate,
rather than something that moves with their mood or how the day has gone.

So the honest version of "breathe at six a minute" is: six is a good place to start, your own
best rate is probably within a breath or two either side of it, and the way to find it is to
try a few and notice which one feels like it takes the least effort to keep going.

::: {.hands}
[For your hands]{.t}
If six feels wrong for someone — strained, or oddly effortful — that is worth taking at face
value rather than as a failure to relax. Try five and try seven. Bigger people tend to sit
at the slower end.
:::
